messages.subject: general question about entropy
parts:
Hi everybody,

My understanding of entropy is that it's the uncertainty in a scenario, so if there are equal chances of an outcome occurring, entropy is at its maximum because there's no way we could predict an outcome. Following this logic, why is it that noisy signals trend higher in the acoustic entropy index compared to simpler waveforms? If I plot the PMF of the amplitude for a simple sine wave, it looks like there is a relatively equal probability of any one amplitude occurring. Can someone explain to me what I'm missing?

Thanks

Sean

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] general question about entropy
parts:
Dear Sean,

It is not a seewave question but I will try to reply quickly.

In the original paper where we described the entopy-like indices, we referred to two indices: (1) H[t] deals with the PMF of the amplitude envelope, and (2) H[f] deals with the PMF of the (mean) frequency spectrum.

A pure tone with a square amplitude envelope will return a high H[t] but a low H[f] because the envelope is flat but the frequency spectrum is characterised by a unique frequency peak.
A white noise will have a high H[t] and high H[f] because both envelope and frequency spectrum tend to be flat.

The index H, which multiplies H[t] and H[f], can therefore return mixed results depending on both envelope and spectrum shapes.

HTH a bit,

Jerome
